title: Impact of Word Choice Practice 2
description: 4 short texts - 8 focused impact of word choice questions
subject: rla
passage:
TEXT A - Old Bridge

The writer says rust crept across the steel beams over decades.

TEXT B - Customer Service

The report says complaints spiked after the update.

TEXT C - Trail Description

The trail clings to the hillside for the final kilometer.

TEXT D - Policy Draft

The draft says staff should verify the address before sending confidential records.

questions.explanation: Crept suggests slow movement that is easy to overlook.
questions.rule: Use the exact wording and surrounding context as evidence.

options.text: a sense of slow, gradual spread
a precise measure of how far the rust traveled across the beams
options.whyWrong: “Crept” gives an impression of movement, not a measurable distance.

options.text: a sudden spread that happened after one major failure
options.whyWrong: “Crept” suggests slow gradual change over the stated decades.

options.text: a positive sense that the bridge is adapting naturally as it ages
options.whyWrong: The word makes deterioration feel gradual and encroaching, not positive.

questions.prompt: If spread replaced crept, what would be lost?
questions.explanation: Spread gives the fact without the same manner of movement.
questions.rule: Use the exact wording and surrounding context as evidence.

options.text: the fact that the rust eventually covered more of the steel
options.whyWrong: “Spread” would still preserve the idea that rust extended across the beams; what it loses is the slow, creeping quality.

options.text: the fact that the change happened over decades
options.whyWrong: The sentence still explicitly says “over decades,” even if “crept” is replaced.

options.text: the information that the beams are made of steel
options.whyWrong: Changing the verb would not remove the stated material.

options.text: the slow, stealthy quality

questions.explanation: Spiked describes a rapid and steep rise.
questions.rule: Use the exact wording and surrounding context as evidence.

options.text: To suggest complaints became physically dangerous after the update.
options.whyWrong: “Spiked” is figurative and describes the amount changing sharply.

options.text: To emphasize a sudden sharp increase.
To imply the update was quickly removed because users objected.
options.whyWrong: The sentence reports complaint volume, not what happened to the update afterward.

options.text: To make the report sound pleased about the increase.
options.whyWrong: A spike in complaints is presented as a sharp change, not a positive outcome.

questions.explanation: Rose is the most neutral description of increase.
questions.rule: Use the exact wording and surrounding context as evidence.

options.text: rose
shot up
options.whyWrong: “Shot up” keeps a strong sudden increase rather than softening it.

options.text: surged
options.whyWrong: “Surged” still strongly emphasizes a rapid increase; “rose” is the more neutral reduction in intensity.

options.text: exploded
options.whyWrong: “Exploded” is more dramatic than “spiked,” not less intense.

questions.explanation: Clings creates a vivid image of the trail staying close to the hillside.
questions.rule: Use the exact wording and surrounding context as evidence.

options.text: that hikers have difficulty moving because the trail is too narrow
options.whyWrong: The sentence describes the trail’s relationship to the hillside, not hikers being unable to move.

options.text: that the trail is physically attached to the hill by an adhesive material
options.whyWrong: “Clings” is figurative and describes how closely the route follows the slope.

options.text: how closely the trail follows a steep slope
that the hillside becomes less steep during the final kilometer
options.whyWrong: “Clings” suggests a close relationship to a steep slope rather than flattening terrain.

questions.prompt: How would follows change the sentence?
questions.explanation: Follows communicates route but not the same tight, precarious image.
questions.rule: Use the exact wording and surrounding context as evidence.

options.text: It would imply that the trail becomes physically longer.
options.whyWrong: Changing the verb affects vividness, not length.

options.text: It would suggest the trail has been closed to hikers.
options.whyWrong: Neither verb implies closure.

options.text: It would make the hillside sound steeper than “clings” does.
options.whyWrong: “Follows” is the more neutral verb and removes some of the vivid steep-slope impression.

options.text: It would be more neutral and less vivid.

questions.prompt: Why is verify more precise than check?
questions.explanation: Verify specifically means confirm that something is correct.
questions.rule: Use the exact wording and surrounding context as evidence.

options.text: It suggests taking a quick look is enough even if the address may be wrong.
options.whyWrong: “Verify” requires confirming accuracy rather than a casual glance.

options.text: It emphasizes confirming accuracy.
It means staff should remove the address before sending the records.
options.whyWrong: Verification checks correctness; it does not mean deletion.

options.text: It requires asking the customer to change addresses before any records can be sent.
options.whyWrong: The policy says confirm the existing address, not require a move or change.

questions.prompt: What is the main effect of the more precise verb?
questions.explanation: Precise word choice reduces ambiguity about what staff must do.
questions.rule: Use the exact wording and surrounding context as evidence.

options.text: It makes the policy sound optional because staff can decide how carefully to check.
options.whyWrong: More precise wording makes the required action clearer, not more optional.

options.text: It changes which confidential records the policy applies to.
options.whyWrong: The verb clarifies the action on the address; it does not change the records covered.

options.text: It makes the required action clearer.
It makes the sentence more emotional by suggesting distrust of customers.
options.whyWrong: “Verify” is procedural and precise, not emotionally accusatory.

curriculum.learningObjective: Apply impact of word choice reasoning across varied original short texts and explain answers from textual evidence.
